extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, physics, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for classifying sciences, judging scientific concepts, and evaluating mechanistic/empirical claims (e.g., inertia, Newton's laws, parsimony, evidence standards). Focus is on principles of scientific method and standards for legitimate inference and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best form for classification (branching tree)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Bacon we learn that the best form for classification is that of a branching tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a branching-tree structure when classifying the sciences, but recognise limits: Comte emphasises interdependence among sciences (so clear understanding of one may need prior study of several others), and the classificatory position of a science changes with its development, giving any system only temporary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for interdependence in classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: There is in reality an interdependence in the sciences, so that a clear understanding of one may necessitate a previous study of several others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing classifications or curricula, allow for cross-linkages and prerequisites; avoid strictly isolating branches when conceptual or empirical dependencies exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract vs Concrete distinction (Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the fundamental distinction between Abstract and Concrete Science, those which deal respectively with the modes and the contents of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to structure divisions of knowledge; the author identifies three fundamental divisions (Abstract, Physical, Biological) and notes they are connected pairwise by Applied Mathematics and Biophysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of thought / Occam's razor
rubrics_metrics.description: Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitate (Do not multiply entities beyond necessity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parsimony as a canon of scientific thought: prefer explanations that assume no more causes or more onerous causes than necessary. Beware of converting the axiom into metaphysical dogma (e.g., projecting 'simplicity' or 'perfection' beyond sense-impression). Hamilton's stronger metaphysical formulations should be avoided in scientific contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neither more nor more onerous causes than necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither more, nor more onerous, causes are to be assumed, than are necessary to account for the phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fuller operational form of parsimony: when choosing among hypotheses prefer those with fewer assumptions and lighter causal commitments; avoid introducing entities or causes solely to preserve a preferred metaphysical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of a conception: deducibility from perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception must be deducible from the perceptions; scientific validity of a conception depends on this deducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that conceptual constructs used in theory are grounded in perceptual (empirical) data or in demonstrably deducible transformations of such data; avoid purely speculative constructs that cannot be connected to perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and canons of legitimate inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference: the scientific validity of an inference; limits of legitimate inference; canons of legitimate inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply explicit canons (e.g., criteria in pages 71-73 referenced) when making inductive or deductive inferences; recognise the boundaries beyond which inference becomes unjustified conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remain agnostic when alternatives remain possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If it has not been shown that no other sufficient perceptual formula can be found, the true scientific method is to remain agnostic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not posit extraordinary causes (e.g., spirit hierarchies) simply because one explanation looks insufficient; first attempt to find other perceptual/formulaic explanations and only adopt new ontologies when all empirically adequate alternatives are eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perceptual from conceptual spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse the perceptual and the conceptual: e.g., force, sense-impression, moving ideals and modes of their motion must be kept distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing from observations to high-level theorising, maintain conceptual clarity about what is a sense-impression (empirical datum) and what is a theoretical construct; conflating them leads to illegitimate metaphysical inferences (illustrated in the critique of Wallace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret experiments in unison with known facts (Mach's caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: We can only interpret the case as it is presented to us in different ways; when an interpretation contradicts experience we have interpreted it falsely. We must bring experiments into unison with other facts known to us and not with arbitrary imaginings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate experimental interpretations by their consistency with the broader empirical corpus; thought experiments (e.g., Newton's bucket) should be tied back to measurable consequences and allied facts before being taken to support sweeping ontological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixity of direction and operational definition of rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: A line the points of which are conceived as having no relative accelerations in the direction of the line is defined as having a fixed direction in space; spin/rotation is described when relative accelerations of parts manifest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define rotation operationally in terms of observable consequences (relative accelerations, centrifugal effects, flattening at poles, changes in apparent gravity). Use conceivable experiments (even if impossible in practice) to clarify definitions, but rely on measurable collateral effects for empirical adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in inferring absolute motion from local experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not follow that Newton's extension of the principle to the planetary system leads us to an absolute motion in an absolute space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware attributing absolute frames from local phenomena; consider alternative relational interpretations (as Mach argues) and test by comparing with other empirical indicators (e.g., stellar reference frames, gravity variations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of evidence for extraordinary historical biological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of maximum period of seed vitality is unsettled because long experiments are slow and well-authenticated ancient examples are rare; many claimed cases lack legal-level provenance or proper experimental verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require robust provenance and direct experimental verification for claims of extraordinary biological persistence (e.g., seeds centuries old). Distinguish between anecdotal/archaeological reports and botanical/experimental proof; note that long-duration experiments and chain-of-custody are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution extending macroscopic laws to molecules/atoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater caution is necessary than sometimes observed in extending Newton's third law and other macroscopic laws to molecules or atoms, which may have oscillatory or translatory velocities relative to an intervening ether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not uncritically generalise classical mechanical laws to microphysics without accounting for medium effects, finite propagation times, non-collinearity of mutual accelerations, or the kinetic contributions of intervening media; treat molecular/atomic domains as requiring separate empirical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for mediating media and time delays in action explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent action at a distance may be due to kinetic energy of an intervening ether; changes in one corpuscle would not be immediately felt by a distant corpuscle — time would be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating force models, consider models with mediating media and finite propagation speed; prefer explanations that include mechanisms for transmission and allow for measurable time-lags or field-mediated interactions rather than instantaneous action-at-a-distance assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and operational grounding of 'force' and 'mass'
rubrics_metrics.description: Force as a cause has scientific definitions (redistribution, resultant); mass can be defined as the ratio of the number of units in two accelerations (mass via accelerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use operational definitions tied to measurement when introducing fundamental quantities: define mass and force in terms of accelerations, interactions, and measurement procedures rather than as metaphysical primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disciplined imagination in scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination should be used in a disciplined and scientific way to construct hypotheses and conceptual models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage imaginative hypothesis generation, but require that imaginative constructs be constrained by empirical deducibility, parsimony, and the canons of legitimate inference; avoid unfettered speculation that cannot be tied to perceptions or testable consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony limited to scientific economy, not metaphysical dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as these axioms are valuable as canons of thought they express no dogma but a fundamental principle of the economy of thought; when extended into claims like 'Natura horret superfluum' they pass into metaphysical dogma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying parsimony, confine it to methodological economy in scientific explanations; resist elevating it to a metaphysical principle about nature's alleged simplicity or perfection.
